The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾, meaning Adam.

﴿Then from a drop (nutfah)﴾, meaning his offspring.

﴿Then from a clinging clot (alaqah)﴾, meaning that the drop becomes a clot in the womb.

﴿Then from a lump of flesh (mudghah)﴾, meaning that the clot becomes a lump of flesh, which is the amount of flesh that can be chewed.

﴿Formed and unformed﴾. There are four interpretations of this:

The first: the "formed" is what has become a created form, and the "unformed" is the drops that the wombs expelled without them becoming a created form. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: its meaning is fully formed and not fully formed. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: its meaning is shaped and unshaped, like a miscarriage. This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: it means the one complete in its months and the one not complete. This was said by al-Dahhak. The poet said:

*Is it for the unformed that weeping is done? Then where is resolve, woe to you, and modesty?*

﴿That We may make clear to you﴾, meaning in the Qur'an, the beginning of your creation and the transitions of your states.

﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will for a specified term﴾. Mujahid said: until completion.

﴿Then We bring you out as infants; then that you may reach your maturity (ashudd)﴾. We have already mentioned the number of years of ashudd.

﴿And among you is one who is taken in death﴾. There are two possibilities regarding this:

One: meaning before reaching the lowest state of old age.

The second: before reaching the age of ashudd.

﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾. There are three possibilities regarding this:

One: senility, which is the view of Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: to a state like his condition when he came out from his mother's belly, related by al-Naqqash.

The third: the loss of reason, said by al-Yazidi.

﴿So that he will not know, after knowledge, anything﴾. There are two possibilities regarding this:

One: he does not acquire knowledge of what he previously knew.

The second: after his former reason, he does not understand anything.

In my view, a third possibility is also admissible: that he does not act upon his knowledge at all. Here action is expressed by knowledge, because the effect of old age on action is more pronounced than its effect on knowledge.

﴿And you see the earth lifeless (hamidah)﴾. There are three interpretations regarding this:

One: dust-colored (ghabra'), which is the view of Qatadah.

The second: dry, not producing anything, which is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The third: that it is worn out and faded; hudud means decay, and from this is the line of al-A'sha:

*Qutaylah said: "What ails your body, looking so pale?" And I see your garments worn and faded.*

﴿Then when We send down water upon it, it stirs (ihtazzat) and swells (rabat)﴾. Regarding ﴿ihtazzat﴾ there are two possibilities:

(p-9) One: its meaning is that it caused growth to sprout. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The second: its meaning is that its vegetation stirred, and its stirring is the intensity of its movement, as the poet said:

*She sways when she stands, and quivers when she walks, as the branch of the ban-tree quivers amid green leaves.*

Regarding ﴿rabat﴾ there are two possibilities:

One: its meaning is that its vegetation was multiplied.

The second: its meaning is that it swelled due to the appearance of its growth. According to this second view, there is an inversion of order (taqdim and ta'khir), and its intended sense is: "When We send down water upon it, it swells and stirs." This is the view of al-Hasan and Abu Ubaydah. According to the first view, there is no inversion or displacement.

﴿And it causes to grow from every beautiful pair﴾. Regarding this there are two possibilities:

One: meaning from every kind. This is the view of Ibn Shajarah.

The second: from every color, due to the differences in the colors of plants: green, red, and yellow.

﴿Beautiful (bahij)﴾ means of good appearance.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verse 8–10:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿turning aside, twisting his side﴾, has two interpretations:

The first: one who twists his neck in aversion from Allah and His Messenger. This is the saying of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is one who twists his neck out of arrogance in refusing to respond. This is the saying of Ibn Abbas.

Al-Mufaddal said: al-i'tf (ʿiṭf) is the side, and from it comes the expression "so-and-so looks at his aṭrāf (sides)," meaning at his flanks.

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

﴿So that he may lead astray from the way of Allah﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: his denial of the Messenger and his turning away from his sayings.

The second (p-10): when one of his people wished to enter Islam, he would bring him in, detain him, make conditions for him, rebuke him, and say, "This is better for you than what Muhammad calls you to." This was related by al-Dahhak.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 11–13:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And among people is he who worships Allah on an edge﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

The first: it means "on doubt" (washk), and this is the saying of Mujahid, because he is inclined between faith and disbelief.

The second: "on a condition," and this is the saying of Ibn Kamil.

The third: "on weakness in worship," like standing "on an edge" (harf), and this is the saying of Ali ibn Isa.

In my view, a fourth interpretation is possible: that the edge (harf) of a thing is a part of it, so it is as if he worships Allah with his tongue while disobeying Him in his heart.

﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face﴾. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: that this was revealed concerning some tribes of the Arabs and the people of the villages around Madinah, who would say: "We come to Muhammad (ﷺ); if we find good, we follow him, and if not, we return to our families." This is the saying of Ibn Jurayj. So Allah, exalted, revealed: ﴿If good befalls him, he is content with it﴾. It may also bear two other meanings:

(p-11) One of them: he is content with the good because of his faith.

The second: his soul is at rest with his station.

﴿And if a trial befalls him﴾, that is, a affliction in himself, his child, or his wealth.

﴿He turns back on his face﴾. In my view this may bear two meanings:

One of them: he reverts from his religion as an apostate.

The second: he returns to his people in fear.

﴿He has lost the world and the Hereafter﴾. He loses the world by departing from it, and he loses the Hereafter by his hypocrisy.

﴿That is the manifest loss﴾, that is, clear in the corruption of his immediate state and the passing of what is to come.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Wretched is the protector, and wretched is the companion﴾. He means the idol. In this there are two interpretations:

One of them: al-mawla is the helper and al-ashir is the companion, and this is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The second: al-mawla is the one worshipped and al-ashir is the close associate, and from this it is said of the husband that he is ashir because of his mixing (khiltah), derived from mu'ashara (living together).

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And whomever Allah humiliates, there is no one to honor him﴾. In it there are two aspects (wajhan):

The first: And whomever Allah humiliates, by sending him to the Fire, there is no one to honor him by admitting him to Paradise.

﴿Indeed, Allah does what He wills﴾ of reward and punishment. This is the view of Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: And whomever Allah humiliates through wretchedness (al-shiqwa), there is no one to honor him through happiness (al-sa'ada).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And the Sacred Mosque which We have made for the people﴾, has two interpretations.

The first: He meant the Mosque itself. The meaning of His saying ﴿which We have made for the people﴾ is: a qiblah for their prayer and a place of rites (manasik) for their Hajj.

﴿Equal therein are the resident and the visitor﴾: the resident (al-'Akif) is the one who stays there, and the visitor (al-Bad) is the one who comes to it from elsewhere. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-16) The second view: the Sacred Mosque refers to the entire Haram. On this view, regarding His saying ﴿which We have made for the people, equal therein are the resident and the visitor﴾, there are two aspects:

The first: they are equal in its houses and dwellings, and the resident who stays there has no greater claim to them than the visitor who travels there. This is the view of Mujahid and of those who forbade the sale of the houses of Makkah, such as Abu Hanifah.

The second: they are equal in that whoever enters it is secure, and one may not kill game (sayd) within it, nor cut its trees (ya'du).

﴿And whoever intends therein deviation (ilhad) with wrongdoing, We will make him taste of a painful punishment﴾. Al-Ilhad means inclining away from the truth. The letter ba' in His saying ﴿bi-ilhadin﴾ is superfluous (za'idah), like its occurrence in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a tree grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20], and like it in the saying of the poet:

"We are the sons of Ja'dah, the people of al-Falaj; we strike with the sword and hope for relief (bi-l-faraj)."

That is, we hope for relief (al-faraj), so the sense of the statement is: and whoever intends therein deviation with wrongdoing.

Regarding deviation with wrongdoing there are four interpretations:

The first: it is associating partners with Allah, by worshipping other than Allah therein. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: it is making lawful what is forbidden therein. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: making lawful what is forbidden therein deliberately. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is hoarding food in Makkah. This is the view of Hassan ibn Thabit.

Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and his companions when they barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from his 'umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah.(p-17)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 26–27:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And when We settled for Abraham the place of the House﴾, has two interpretations:

The first: its meaning is "We made the place of the House ready for him." This is related from Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: its meaning is "We made the place of the House known to him by a sign by which he could be guided."

Concerning the sign there are two opinions:

The first: this was said by Qutrub. A cloud was sent, and it hovered directly over the Kaʿba, and he built according to its shade.

The second: this was said by al-Suddi. The sign was a wind that blew and swept around the House, called al-Khujuj.

﴿That you shall not associate anything with Me﴾, i.e., do not worship alongside Me any god other than Me.

﴿And purify My House﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: from shirk and the worship of idols. This is the saying of Qatada.

The second: from impurities, dung and blood that had been cast around the House. Ibn ʿIsa mentioned this.

The third: from false speech. This is the saying of Yahya ibn Salam.

﴿For those who circumambulate, and those who stand [in prayer], and bow and prostrate﴾. As for "those who circumambulate," it refers to the House. Concerning "those who stand," there are two opinions:

The first: it means those standing in prayer. This is the saying of ʿAta.

The second: those who reside in Makkah. This is the saying of Qatada.

﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾ means in prayer, and in this is evidence for the reward of prayer in the House.

Al-Dahhak related that when Abraham reached the foundations of the House, he found a tablet on which was written: "I am Allah, Lord of Bakka. I created good and evil. Blessed is the one for whose hands I have decreed good, and woe to the one for whose hands I have decreed evil."

Some of the scholars of spiritual insights (ashab al-khawatir) interpreted His saying, ﴿And purify My House﴾, as meaning the hearts.

﴿For those who circumambulate﴾ means the pilgrims of Allah; ﴿and those who stand﴾ means faith; ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾ means fear and hope.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾, means: inform them and call out to them in truth. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: this statement is a report of Allah's command, may He be glorified, to His Prophet Abraham. It is related that Abraham climbed Mount Abu Qubays and said: "Servants of Allah, indeed Allah, glorified and exalted, has built a House and has commanded you to make pilgrimage to it, so make pilgrimage." Whoever was in the loins of men and the wombs of women responded: "At Your service, O Lord, at Your service."

No one will make pilgrimage to it until the Day of Resurrection except those who answered the call of Abraham. It is said that the first to respond were the people of Yemen, and they are the most numerous of people in pilgrimage to it.

The second: this is a command from Allah, exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to command the people to make pilgrimage to the House.

﴿They will come to you on foot﴾, i.e., walking on their feet; "rijal" is the plural of "rajil" (one who walks).

﴿And on every lean camel﴾, i.e., a lean camel, which is emaciated. He said "lean" because it does not reach it except having become lean.

﴿They will come from every deep mountain pass﴾, i.e., distant. From this is the saying of the poet:

Playing among them with the burning coal, a far-reaching, deep sinew-stretch.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 28–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: that it refers to witnessing the places of standing (at 'Arafat and Muzdalifah) and performing the rites (manasik, the ritual acts of Hajj).

Second: that it refers to forgiveness of their sins. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: that it refers to trade in this world and reward in the Hereafter. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days﴾. Regarding these there are three opinions:

First: that they are the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last of which is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, and it is the position (madhhab) of al-Shafi'i.

Second: that they are the three days of tashriq. This is the view of 'Ata' al-'Awfi.

Third: that they are the Day of Tarwiyah, the Day of 'Arafah, and the Day of Sacrifice. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

﴿over what He has provided for them of the livestock animals﴾, meaning: over the slaughter of what He has provided for them of the livestock animals, namely the eight pairs (al-azwaj al-thamaniyah) of sacrificial animals (al-dahaya) and offerings (al-hada ya).

﴿So eat from them and feed the miserable, the poor﴾. Regarding eating and feeding there are three aspects:

First: that eating and feeding are both obligatory, and it is not permissible to neglect either of them. This is the view of Abu al-Tayyib ibn Salamah.

Second: that eating and feeding are both recommended (mustahabb), and one may suffice with whichever of them he wishes. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas ibn Suraij.

Third: that eating is recommended and feeding is obligatory. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. If he feeds all of it, it suffices him; if he eats all of it, it does not suffice him. This applies to what is voluntary (tatawwu'). As for obligatory blood sacrifices (wajibat al-dima'), it is not permissible for us to eat from them.

Regarding ﴿the miserable, the poor﴾ there are five aspects:

First: that the poor man is one who has a disability (zamanah), and this is the view of Mujahid.

Second: the poor man is one who is afflicted by the harm of hunger.

Third: the poor man is one upon whom the trace of destitution (al-bu's) has appeared.

Fourth: he is the one who extends his hand in requesting and seeks by begging (yatakaffaf bi al-talab).

Fifth: he is the one who abstains from being sat with (yu'naf 'an mujalasatih).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Then let them end their state of disarray (tafath)﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

First: the rites of Hajj. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar.

Second: shaving the head. This is the view of Qatadah, and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"They shaved their heads, not shaving away their tafath,"

. . . . . . . .

Third: throwing the pebbles at the jamarat (ramy al-jimar). This is the view of Mujahid.

Fourth: removing the untidiness of ihram by trimming the nails, taking hair, washing, and using perfume. This is the view of al-Hasan.

It was said to one of the righteous scholars: what is the meaning of the dishevelment of the muhrim? He said: so that Allah, exalted is He, may witness from you turning away from caring for yourself, so He knows your sincerity in giving it up for His obedience.

al-Hasan was asked about being stripped (al-tajarrud) in Hajj, and he said: strip your heart of heedlessness, your self of frivolity, and your tongue of idle talk; then you may do as you wish.

The poet said:

"They ended their tafath and their vow, then they went on toward Najd, and they did not wait for 'Ali."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 28–29:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: that it refers to witnessing the places of standing (at 'Arafat and Muzdalifah) and performing the rites (manasik, the ritual acts of Hajj).

Second: that it refers to forgiveness of their sins. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: that it refers to trade in this world and reward in the Hereafter. This is the view of Mujahid.

﴿And mention the name of Allah on known days﴾. Regarding these there are three opinions:

First: that they are the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, the last of which is the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, and it is the position (madhhab) of al-Shafi'i.

Second: that they are the three days of tashriq. This is the view of 'Ata' al-'Awfi.

Third: that they are the Day of Tarwiyah, the Day of 'Arafah, and the Day of Sacrifice. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

First: that eating and feeding are both obligatory, and it is not permissible to neglect either of them. This is the view of Abu al-Tayyib ibn Salamah.

Second: that eating and feeding are both recommended (mustahabb), and one may suffice with whichever of them he wishes. This is the view of Abu al-'Abbas ibn Suraij.

Third: that eating is recommended and feeding is obligatory. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. If he feeds all of it, it suffices him; if he eats all of it, it does not suffice him. This applies to what is voluntary (tatawwu'). As for obligatory blood sacrifices (wajibat al-dima'), it is not permissible for us to eat from them.

Regarding ﴿the miserable, the poor﴾ there are five aspects:

First: that the poor man is one who has a disability (zamanah), and this is the view of Mujahid.

Second: the poor man is one who is afflicted by the harm of hunger.

Third: the poor man is one upon whom the trace of destitution (al-bu's) has appeared.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 22, verses 30–31:**

(p-22) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is so. And whoever honors the sacred rites of God, it is better for him with his Lord.﴾ On this there are two opinions:

The first: it means performing what He commanded of the rites (*manasik*) of the pilgrimage. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: it means refraining from what He forbade during his state of *ihram* (the sacred state of pilgrimage).

In my view, a third opinion is also possible: honoring His sacred things means that one performs obedience and enjoins it, and refrains from disobedience and forbids it.

﴿And the grazing livestock has been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you.﴾ On this there are two opinions:

The first: except what is recited to you of the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen from a height, the gored, and what the beast of prey has eaten, *except what you slaughter*, and what is sacrificed on the *nusub* (stone altars).

The second: except what is recited to you, not hunting game while you are in a state of *ihram*.

﴿So avoid the filth of the idols.﴾ On this there are two interpretations:

(p-22) The first: the meaning is, avoid the filth *from* the idols, and the filth of idols is worshipping them. So its meaning becomes: avoid worshipping idols.

The second: its meaning is: avoid the idols, for they are a form of filth.

﴿And avoid the word of falsehood.﴾ On this there are four sayings:

The first: it is polytheism (*shirk*). This is the saying of Yahya ibn Salam.

The second: it is lying. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: it is false testimony. Ayman ibn Muhammad narrated: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood up delivering a sermon and said: 'O people, false testimony has been made equal to associating partners with God,' twice. Then he recited: ﴿So avoid the filth of the idols and avoid the word of falsehood.﴾"

The fourth: it is the worship of the polytheists. This was related by al-Naqqash.

In my view, a fifth saying is also possible: it is hypocrisy, because it is Islam outwardly and falsehood inwardly.

(p-23) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ḥunafā’ for God.﴾ On this there are four interpretations:

The first: it means submitting (*muslimīn*) to God. This is the saying of al-Dahhak. Dhu al-Rummah said:

*When the shade turns in the evening, you see him a ḥanīf,*
*and at the height of forenoon he becomes a Christian.*

The second: sincerely devoted (*mukhliṣīn*) to God. This is the saying of Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: upright (*mustaqīmīn*) for God. This is the saying of Ali ibn Isa.

The fourth: pilgrims (*ḥujjājan*) to God. This is the saying of Qutrub.

﴿Not associating anything with Him.﴾ On this there are two meanings:

The first: not showing off in His worship before any of His creatures.

The second: not associating anyone with Him in the *talbiyah* (the pilgrim's call of "Here I am") of the Hajj. They used to say in their *talbiyah*: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who belongs to You, You own him and what he owns." This was said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 32–33:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿That [is so]. And whoever honors the symbols of Allah﴾, has two interpretations:

One of them: the obligations of Allah.

The second: the markers of His religion (ma'alim din). From this is the saying of al-Kumayt:

Regarding it there are three opinions:

One of them: that they are the rites of the Hajj (manasik al-hajj), and honoring them is marking them (ish'ar), and this is related from a group of scholars.

The second: that they are the marked camels (al-budn al-mush'ira), and honoring them is fattening them and choosing them well, and this is the view of Mujahid.

The third: that they are the whole religion of Allah, and honoring them is adhering to it, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿Indeed, it is from the piety of the hearts﴾. al-Kalbi and al-Suddi said: from the sincerity of the hearts.

In my opinion, it may also carry another meaning: that one intends the reward.

It may also carry yet another meaning: that one seeks what pleases Allah Most High.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿For you therein are benefits until an appointed term﴾, has three opinions:

One of them: that the benefits are trade, and this is the view of those who interpreted the symbols as the rites of the Hajj, and the appointed term is the return (al-'awd).

The second: that the benefits are reward, and the appointed term is the Resurrection (al-qiyama), and this is the interpretation of those who understood them as the religion.

The third: that the benefits are riding, milk and offspring, and this is the view of those who interpreted them as the sacrificial animals (al-hady). According to this, regarding the appointed term there are two views:

One of them: that the benefits are before its designation (al-ijab) and after it, and the appointed term is the slaughter (al-nahr), and this is the view of 'Ata'.

The second: the whole Haram is its place (of sacrifice), and this is the view of al-Shafi'i.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 34–35:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿For every community We have appointed a rite (mansak)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: it means the Hajj (pilgrimage), and this is the saying of Qatada.

(p-25) The second: it means sacrifice (dhabh), and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The third: it means a festival (eid), and this is the saying of al-Kalbi and al-Farra'. In the language of the Arabs, the *mansak* is the customary place, and from it comes the naming of the rites of the Hajj (manasik al-hajj), because of the regular visiting of their places.

﴿That they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided for them of the cattle of grazing animals﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: that they are the hady (sacrificial animals), if it is said that the *mansak* is the Hajj.

The second: that they are the udhiyy (animals sacrificed at Eid), if it is said that the *mansak* is the festival.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And give good tidings to the humble (mukhbitin)﴾. Regarding this there are nine interpretations:

The first: those who are at peace in the remembrance of their Lord, and this is the saying of Mujahid. From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that their hearts humbly submit to Him﴾ [al-Hajj: 54].

The second: its meaning is those who are humble (mutawadi'in), and this is the saying of Qatada.

The third: the submissive (khashi'in), and this is the saying of al-Hasan.

The difference between humility (tawadu') and submissiveness (khushu') is that humility is in character, and submissiveness is in the body.

The fourth: those who fear (khaifin), and this is the meaning of the saying of Yahya ibn Sallam.

The fifth: the sincere (mukhlisin), and this is the saying of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

The sixth: those whose hearts are tender (raqiqah qulubuhum), and this is the saying of al-Kalbi.

The seventh: that they are those who strive diligently in worship, and this is the saying of al-Kalbi and Mujahid.

The eighth: that they are the righteous who are at peace, and this is also related from Mujahid.

The ninth: they are those who do not wrong, and if they are wronged they do not seek retribution, and this is the saying of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad.

(p-٢٦) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the camels, We have made them for you among the symbols of God﴾. Regarding *al-budn* (the camels offered as sacrifice) there are three opinions:

First: they are camels. This is the view of the majority.

Second: they are camels, cows, and sheep. This is the view of Jabir and ʿAtaʾ.

Third: every animal with a hoof, meaning camels, cows, and sheep. This is an anomalous view, related by Ibn al-Shajara. They were called *budn* because they are fattened (*mubaddanah*). "The symbols of God" means His religion according to one of the two interpretations, and His obligations according to the other.

Some of the people of insight went to extremes and interpreted *budn* as purifying your body from innovations (*bidaʿ*), and *shaʿaʾir* as making yourself feel (*tastashʿir*) the fear of God and obedience to Him. This is far-fetched.

﴿For you in them is good﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One: that is, reward. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Two: benefit. If their backs are needed, one rides them; if their milk is milked, it is drunk. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi.

﴿So mention the name of God over them, standing in rows﴾. This is the reading of the majority. Al-Hasan read *ṣawāfiya*, and Ibn Masʿud read *ṣawāfin*.

Interpreting *ṣawāfin* according to the reading of the majority, there are three aspects:

First: lined up (*muṣṭaffah*). This is what Ibn ʿIsa mentioned.

Second: standing, because their forelegs are tied with shackles. This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar.

Third: hobbled (*maʿqūlah*). This is the view of Mujahid.

The interpretation of *ṣawāfiya*, the reading of al-Hasan, is: purely for God Most High, derived from *al-ṣafwa* (the pure, the choice).

The interpretation of *ṣawāfin*, the reading of Ibn Masʿud, is that they are arranged in lines. This means that one of its forelegs is tied until it stands on three legs, derived from *ṣafana al-faras* when a horse bends one of its forelegs until it stands on three. From this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿the swift, well-bred horses﴾ (Q. 38:31). The poet said:

*He has grown accustomed to standing, as though he is always standing on three legs, hobbled.*

﴿So when their sides fall﴾, that is, when their sides fall to the ground. From this comes *wajaba al-ḥāʾiṭ* (the wall fell) when it collapsed, and *wajabat al-shams* (the sun set) when it set for sunset. Aws ibn Hajar said:

*Has the sun not been eclipsed, the light of the day, and the full moon behind the setting mountain?*

﴿Then eat from them﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects:

One: eating from them is obligatory if one offers them voluntarily. This is the view of Abu al-Tayyib ibn Salama.

Two: this is the view of the majority, that it is recommended (*istihbab*) and not obligatory. The command was given because it came after a prohibition (*hazr*), since in the pre-Islamic period they used to forbid themselves to eat them.

﴿And feed the contented and the beggar﴾. Regarding them there are four interpretations:

First: *al-qāniʿ* is the one who asks, and *al-muʿtarr* is the one who presents himself without asking. This is the view of al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn Jubayr. From this is the saying of al-Shammakh:

*A man's wealth, when it sets him right, makes him rich, and it spares his needs more chastely than begging.*

That is, from asking.

Second: *al-qāniʿ* is the one who is content and does not ask, and *al-muʿtarr* is the one who asks. This is the view of Qatada. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Upon their wealthy ones is the provision for whoever seeks them, and among the poor are generosity and giving.*

Third: *al-qāniʿ* is the needy wanderer, and *al-muʿtarr* is the friend who visits. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam. From this is the saying of al-Kumayt:

*Either by habit or by visiting.*

Fourth: *al-qāniʿ* is the one who is greedy, and *al-muʿtarr* is the one who comes to the sacrificed animals seeking meat, because he has no meat. This is the view of ʿIkrima. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Upon the night-visitor who comes seeking, O Umm Malik, when he visits me between my fate and my rock.*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verse 37:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah﴾, has two interpretations:

One of them: Allah does not accept the blood; rather He accepts only piety (taqwa). This is the view of ʿAli ibn ʿIsa.

The second: its meaning is that their flesh and their blood do not ascend to Allah, because in the Jahiliyya, when they slaughtered their camels, they faced the Kaʿba with their blood and laid them down toward the House. The Muslims wished to do the same, so Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah, but piety from you reaches Him﴾, meaning that piety and righteous deeds ascend to Him. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿Thus He has subjected them to you﴾, meaning He made them tractable for you, referring to the livestock.

﴿That you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ admits of two interpretations:

One of them: it means the saying of the Basmala (tasmiya) at the time of slaughter.

The second: that you glorify (Allah) at the time of exiting the state of ihram, in place of the talbiya during ihram.

﴿for having guided you﴾, meaning for having guided you to your Hajj.

﴿And give good news to the doers of good﴾ admits of two interpretations:

One of them: with acceptance.

The second: with Paradise.(p-29)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 22, verses 42–46:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And a deserted well﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: it means empty of its people because of their destruction.

Second: its water has sunk deep.

Third: it is left idle, without anyone to draw from it or ropes and buckets for it.

﴿And a lofty palace﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: al-mashid (المَشِيدُ) means the fortified, and this is the view of al-Kalbi. From it comes the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And Tayma', in which he left no trunk of a palm tree, nor any fortress, except that it was flattened with stones.*

Second: al-mashid means the high, and this is the view of Qatada. From it comes the saying of Adi ibn Zayd:

*He built it of marble and covered it with gypsum, so that for the birds there are nests on its heights.*

Third: al-mashid means plastered with lime, and al-shid (الشِّيدُ) is lime plaster. This is the view of Ikrima and Mujahid. From it comes the saying of al-Tirimmah:

*Like a water serpent between the mud and the plaster.*

In the sentence there is an implied elided element, and its estimated form is: "and a lofty palace, like it, is left idle." It is also said that the palace and the well are both well known in Hadramawt in the land of Yemen. The palace overlooks the top of a mountain, and no one can ascend to it by any means. The well is at its foot, and the wind does not allow anything that falls into it to remain, but casts it out. The people of the palaces were the kings of the settled lands, and the people of the wells were the kings of the desert, meaning: We destroyed these and those.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth, so that they would have hearts with which they understand?﴾ This indicates two matters: that intellect is knowledge, and that its seat is the heart.

In His saying ﴿with which they understand﴾ there are two interpretations:

First: "with which they act," because the eyes see and the hearts direct.

﴿Or ears with which they hear﴾, meaning, with which they comprehend what they heard of the reports of the earlier generations.

﴿Indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind.﴾ In my view this allows two interpretations:

First: the eyes do not go blind to guidance, but the hearts go blind to being guided.

Second: indeed, the eyes do not go blind to reflection, but the hearts go blind to remembrance.

Mujahid said: Every person has four eyes: two eyes in his head for his worldly life, and two eyes in his heart for his afterlife. If the two eyes of his head go blind but the two eyes of his heart see, his blindness does not harm him at all. If the two eyes of his head see but the two eyes of his heart go blind, his sight does not benefit him at all.

Qatada said: This verse was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind man, who was Abdullah ibn Za'ida.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verse 52–54:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke [or desired, tamanna], Satan cast [something] into his desire (umniyyah)﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: it means that when he recited in his soul (hadatha nafsahu), Satan cast into his soul. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The second: when he recited (qara'a), Satan cast into his recitation. This was said by Qatadah and Mujahid. The poet said:

Who desired the Book of God at the first of his night and its last, met the death-cry of the decrees.

Regarding ﴿messenger or prophet﴾ there are two views:

The first: that the messenger (rasul) and the prophet (nabi) are one, and there is no distinction between the messenger and the prophet. He combined them because the prophets are specific to humankind, whereas the messengers are general to the angels and humankind.

The second view: that they are different, and that the messenger is higher in rank than the prophet.

The one who held this view differed about the distinction between the messenger and the prophet in three sayings:

The first: the messenger is the one to whom the angels descend with revelation, while the prophet is revealed to in his sleep.

The second: the messenger is the one sent to a community, while the prophet is the one who is spoken to (muhaddath) and is not sent to a community. This was said by Qutrub.

The third: the messenger is the one who initiates the laying down of laws and rulings, while the prophet is the one who preserves the law of God. This was said by al-Jahiz.

﴿Then God abolishes what Satan casts﴾, that is, He removes it (yarfa'uhu).

﴿Then God makes His verses firm﴾, that is, He establishes them (yuthbituha). The people of interpretation differed regarding what the Prophet (ﷺ) recited of that, in four sayings:

The first: Satan cast it upon his tongue, and he recited it while heedless.

The second: he was drowsy, so Satan cast it upon his tongue, and he recited it in his drowsiness. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: some of the hypocrites recited it, through the seduction of Satan, so it appeared to the people that it was from the recitation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This was related by Ibn Isa.

The fourth: he only said, "They are the exalted cranes (al-gharaniq al-ula), meaning the angels, and their intercession is indeed hoped for," that is, in your saying. This was said by al-Hasan.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what is narrated: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent down Surah al-Najm, he recited it in the Sacred Mosque until he reached ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza? And Manat, the third, the other [one]﴾ [al-Najm 53:19–20], Satan cast upon his tongue: 'Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is indeed hoped for.' Then he finished the surah and prostrated. The Muslims and the polytheists prostrated with him. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira raised a handful of dust to his forehead and prostrated upon it, for he was an elderly man who could not prostrate. The disbelievers of Quraysh were pleased with this, and whoever had emigrated to the land of Abyssinia heard of it."

Then Jibril denounced to the Prophet (ﷺ) what he had recited, and it grieved him, so God Most High sent down: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke, Satan cast [something] into his desire﴾.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿That He may make what Satan casts a trial﴾. In this there are two meanings: the first, a trial (mihnah).

The second, a test (ikhtibar).

﴿For those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is, hypocrisy.

﴿And the hard of heart﴾, meaning the polytheists.

﴿And indeed the wrongdoers are in extreme schism﴾. In this there are two meanings:

The first: they are in far-reaching error, said by al-Suddi.

The second: they are in a far-off separation from the truth until the Day of Resurrection, said by Yahya ibn Sallam.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 58–60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is so. And whoever retaliates with the like of what he was afflicted with﴾ [the verse], there are two opinions concerning it.

One of them: it was revealed concerning a group of the polytheists of Quraysh who encountered a group of the Muslims on the last two nights of al-Muharram (the sacred month). They attacked them, and the Muslims implored them not to fight them in the sacred month, but they refused. Then Allah granted victory to the Muslims, and this was revealed concerning them. This is related by al-Naqqash.

The second: it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who mutilated a group of Muslims whom they had killed on the Day of Uhud, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) retaliated against them with the like of it, and this was revealed concerning them. This is related by Ibn ʿĪsa.

And the help of Allah (nasr Allah) in this world is through overpowering and subjugation, and in the Hereafter through proof and evidence.

O people, a parable is presented, so listen to it. [Al-Mawardi:] Because God's proofs against them by means of parables are closer to their understanding. If it is said: where is the parable that was presented? There are two views concerning it:

﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke besides God﴾ may bear three meanings: (p-40) One of them: they are the idols that they worshipped besides God.

The second: they are the masters who diverted them from obedience to God.

The third: they are the devils who drove them to disobey God.

﴿Will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it.﴾ This is to inform them that worship is due only to the Creator, the Originator, not to the created, the brought-into-being. He singled out the fly for four matters that pertain to it: its lowliness, its weakness, its repulsiveness, and its abundance. It was named dhubab (fly) because it is driven away (yudhabbu) out of contempt and disgust.

﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them anything, they could not rescue it from it.﴾ This may bear two meanings:

One of them: its spoiling of their fruits and their food until it takes them away from them.

The second: its pain in gnawing at their bodies. So if this, which is the weakest and most contemptible of animals, is something that those they worship besides God cannot create the like of, nor repel its harm, how then could they be gods worshipped and lords obeyed? One of them: that it refers to the worshipper and the worshipped, so its meaning has two views:

One of them: that it refers to the worshipper and the worshipped.

The second: the worshipper and the worshipped are subdued.

The second possibility: that it refers to the one who snatches away, so its meaning has two views:

One of them: the weakness of the snatcher in his power, and of the snatched in his helper.

The second: the snatcher is weakened by humiliation, and the snatched by abjection.

The second: they did not know Him with His true knowledge. This was said by al-Akhfash.

The third: they did not describe Him with His true description. This was said by Qutrub.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 75–76:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, has three interpretations:

First: "What is before them" refers to what existed before the creation of the angels and the prophets, and "what is behind them" refers to what will occur after their creation. This is related from Ibn ʿIsa.

Second: "What is before them" refers to their first deeds, and "what is behind them" refers to their last deeds. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri).

Third: "What is before them" refers to matters of the Hereafter, and "what is behind them" refers to matters of this world. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: "What is before them" refers to matters of the heavens, and "what is behind them" refers to matters of the earth.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 22, verses 77–78:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And strive for Allah with the striving due to Him﴾. al-Suddi said: "Work for Allah with the work due to Him." al-Dahhak said: "That He is obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, and thanked and not disbelieved."

This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]. Scholars differed over whether it has been abrogated (naskh) into two opinions. One of them: it has been abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

(p-42) The second: its ruling remains in force, because "the striving due to Him" is that in which hardship is removed. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best of your religion is the easiest of it."

﴿He has chosen you﴾, i.e., He selected you for His religion.

﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship﴾, meaning any narrowness. In this there are five aspects:

The first: that it is the deliverance from sins through repentance.

The second: the way out of oaths through expiation (kaffarah).

The third: that it is the advancing and postponing of the crescent months in fasting, breaking the fast, and the sacrifice; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that He permitted the shortening of prayer and breaking the fast while traveling.

The fifth: that it is general, because there is nothing in the religion of Islam for which there is no way of escaping sin in it.

﴿The religion of your father Abraham﴾. In this there are four aspects:

The first: that He made it easy for you in the religion as He made easy the religion of your father Abraham.

The second: and do good as the deed of your father Abraham.

The third: that the religion of Abraham, which is his faith, is binding on the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) and included within his religion.

The fourth: that we have the allegiance (wilayah) of Abraham, and the rulings of his religion do not bind us.

(p-43) ﴿He named you Muslims before [this] and in this [Qur'an]﴾. In this there are two aspects:

One of them: that Allah named you Muslims before this Qur'an and in this Qur'an; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: that Abraham named you Muslims; this was said by Ibn Zayd, arguing from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from our descendants a Muslim nation [submitting] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128].

﴿That the Messenger may be a witness over you and that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. In this there are two aspects:

One of them: that the Messenger be a witness over you in conveying the message of his Lord to you, and that you be witnesses over the people, conveying to them the message of their Lord just as the Messenger conveyed to you what he conveyed.

The second: that the Messenger be a witness over you concerning your deeds, and that you be witnesses over the people that their messengers have conveyed to them.

﴿So establish the prayer﴾, meaning the obligatory (mafrudah) prayer.

﴿And give zakah﴾, meaning the obligatory (wajibah) zakah.

﴿And hold fast to Allah﴾. In this there are two aspects:

One of them: take refuge in Allah; this is the saying of Ibn Shajarah.

The second: its meaning is hold fast to the religion of Allah; this is the saying of al-Hasan.

﴿He is your Protector (mawla)﴾. In this there are two aspects:

One of them: your Owner.

The second: your Friend who manages your affairs.

﴿An excellent Protector and an excellent Helper﴾, i.e., an excellent Protector when He did not withhold provision from you though you disobeyed Him, and an excellent Helper when He aided you though you obeyed Him.
